tagline: The Caribbean's largest island — a harbour capital, the region's biggest resort coast, and sea links that history switched off.
summary: Cuba is the Caribbean's largest island: Havana's Malecón waterfront and historic harbour, the Varadero resort peninsula ~65 nm east, and a south-coast chain of heritage bays and beach cays (Cienfuegos, Trinidad/Casilda, Cayo Largo). The island once had famous fast sea connections — Key West ferries ran until 1961, and cruise calls returned briefly in 2016–2019 — but today nearly all visitor movement is by long road transfer or small aircraft. The geography itself is a ready-made foiling network: dense electric hops inside each pole, and hybrid corridors linking the poles along 700+ nm of coast.

demand_signals.label: International visitor volume
demand_signals.note: Volumes remain among the Caribbean's largest even in a down cycle, concentrated on Havana and the beach-cay poles

demand_signals.label: Varadero resort pole
demand_signals.note: Marina Gaviota Varadero, around 1,000 berths, is among the largest marinas in the Caribbean — purpose-built waterside infrastructure already in place

demand_signals.label: Withdrawn sea services = stranded demand
demand_signals.value: Key West↔Havana ferries ran until 1961 (~90 nm); US cruise calls 2016–2019 then suspended
demand_signals.note: Fast, direct sea access to Havana existed and was heavily used in both eras — the demand pattern is proven, the service simply vanished
demand_signals.source: Historical record; US cruise-line Cuba programmes 2016–19

demand_signals.label: Existing harbour-ferry habit
demand_signals.value: Havana's lanchita ferries (Habana Vieja ↔ Regla / Casablanca) run daily
demand_signals.note: A working, adopted public water-transit habit inside Havana Bay to modernise with quiet, clean vessels

demand_signals.label: Road-bound resort transfers
demand_signals.value: Havana↔Varadero ~2 hrs by road; Cayo Largo reachable only by air
demand_signals.note: Every major leisure corridor is a long highway transfer or a small-plane hop — the sea is the straight line nobody uses yet

use_cases.title: Havana ↔ Varadero flagship corridor
use_cases.body: The capital-to-resort run (~65 nm along the north coast) replaces a 2-hour Via Blanca road transfer with a smooth coastal flight from Marina Hemingway or Havana harbour to Marina Gaviota — near the top of all-electric range, comfortable for the hybrid.

use_cases.title: Havana Bay water transit, modernised
use_cases.body: Quiet zero-emission shuttles on the historic lanchita crossings (Habana Vieja ↔ Regla ↔ Casablanca) and along the Malecón — upgrading an existing daily habit in a UNESCO-listed harbour city.

use_cases.title: South-coast heritage & cay chain
use_cases.body: Cienfuegos' sheltered bay, Trinidad/Casilda and the isolated beach cay of Cayo Largo (~75 nm offshore, air-only today) form a natural hybrid-foiling chain with no charging infrastructure required at the cays.

use_cases.title: Marina-to-marina premium tier
use_cases.body: Marina Hemingway (Havana) and Marina Gaviota (Varadero) are established large-marina poles; a foiling tender tier serves visiting yachts, dive trips toward Jardines del Rey and event charters along the Malecón.

journeys.today: About 2 hours by taxi or tour bus on the Via Blanca — every resort guest who wants both the city and the beach pays that road toll twice.
journeys.with_navier: A ~65 nm coastal flight past the Malecón and the north-shore beaches, arriving inside the Caribbean's largest marina — smooth, quiet, and direct hotel-jetty service at the Varadero end.

journeys.today: The much-loved but ageing lanchita ferries shuttle commuters and visitors across Havana Bay.
journeys.with_navier: A silent, zero-emission harbour shuttle on the same historic crossings — clean water transit befitting a UNESCO World Heritage harbour.

journeys.today: Cayo Largo is reachable only by small aircraft; there is no sea service from the mainland.
journeys.with_navier: A ~75 nm hybrid foiling run from the Bahía de Cienfuegos out to the cay's beaches and dive sites — opening Cuba's most isolated resort island to the sea without building any shore charging.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Dense all-electric meshes inside each pole: Havana Bay and the Malecón waterfront, the Varadero peninsula and its Cayo Blanco excursion runs (3–8 nm hops between Marina Gaviota, Marina Chapelín and the cays), and Cienfuegos' enclosed bay. Havana↔Varadero (~65 nm) is achievable but near the range edge — flagged for coordinate-level confirmation before becoming a marquee electric leg.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR (700 nm hybrid, no charging-infrastructure dependency) is the natural backbone for Cuba's long coast: Havana ↔ Varadero with full margin, Havana ↔ Cienfuegos/Trinidad (~120–135 nm), Cienfuegos ↔ Cayo Largo (~75–95 nm), and the resort-pole chain east toward Cayo Coco/Jardines del Rey (~150 nm) — none of which require grid investment at the far end.

competitive_landscape: On-water service today runs through the state marine operators — Marlin Marinas and Gaviota — whose catamaran day-excursions (Varadero↔Cayo Blanco seafari trips) and harbour lanchitas prove daily paid demand on the water. But there is no fast point-to-point passenger service anywhere on the island: inter-pole movement is by road or small aircraft, and the famous international sea links of earlier eras are gone. The incumbent footprint is evidence of demand; the network layer simply does not exist yet.

precedents.what: ~$100M, ~100-vessel electric foiling network with JIH Global, 3-year phased rollout, first 5 vessels in 2026
precedents.why_it_matters: Proof that a national-scale, resort-anchored foiling network can be financed and phased — the closest analogue to Cuba's resort-pole geography.

seasonality: Year-round warm-water operations. The dry season (Nov–Apr) brings occasional north-wind 'frentes fríos' that chop up the exposed north coast — exactly the conditions where foiling above the waves preserves schedule and comfort while displacement boats cancel. Hurricane season (Jun–Nov) requires flexible scheduling and safe-harbour planning; Havana Bay, Cienfuegos Bay and the marina basins provide strong shelter.
regulatory_note: Marine operations in Cuba run through state entities — marina and excursion activity via Marlin Marinas and the Gaviota Group, with national maritime authority oversight. International services are additionally subject to each origin country's rules; current United States sanctions restrict US-linked vessels and transactions with Cuba, so any cross-strait or US-touching service depends on the prevailing licensing framework at the time. In-country and third-country-origin operations follow Cuban port-state and tourism regulations.

sources.label: Cuba international visitor arrivals 2024–25 (ONEI via CubaPlus)
